care-support.title: Care and Support in Wales
care-support.action: Identify the correct assessment duty and explain the person’s outcomes and evidence of need.
care-support.record: Apply the relevant Welsh eligibility regulations rather than a test imported from another system. Check participation barriers and the independent professional advocacy requirements. Record the support plan, separate charging decision, unmet needs and review or complaint route. Ask for written reasons and the relevant local-authority review or complaints process. Consider independent advocacy where required to make participation effective. A disagreement over charges should not erase the needs assessment or interim support plan.

mca.title: Mental Capacity Act 2005
mca.action: Specify the decision and record support and evidence against the relevant abilities.
mca.record: Explain the causal connection to impairment if concluding that capacity is lacking. Check any attorney, deputy or advance decision and the scope of its authority. Record best-interests reasoning, consultation, disagreement and the appropriate challenge route. The Court of Protection deals with relevant disputes and decisions. Consider statutory advocacy requirements and specialist advice where serious disagreement or liberty issues arise. A relative’s agreement should not substitute for the required legal analysis.

dols.title: DoLS and Deprivation of Liberty
dols.action: Record the actual setting, restrictions, duration and response to a wish to leave.
dols.record: Use current judgment and Welsh guidance with specialist advice on the applicable legal test. Check the correct authorisation route, representation, conditions and review. Explore less restrictive alternatives and act on objections or changed circumstances. Explain the representative, advocacy and court challenge arrangements that apply. An existing authorisation should be reviewed through the responsible process; do not simply remove safeguards on the basis of a changed summary or training slide.

mha.title: Mental Health in Wales
mha.action: Identify the exact assessment, detention, treatment or Measure duty involved.
mha.record: Use the Welsh Code and current statutory forms and commencement information. For care planning, record outcomes, named services, responsibilities and review. Explain reassessment and advocacy rights appropriate to the person’s eligibility and status. The Mental Health Review Tribunal for Wales and other statutory review routes address particular detention questions. Measure care planning and reassessment are separate rights. Explain which process addresses the person’s concern and how to obtain support or legal advice.

safeguarding.title: Safeguarding Adults in Wales
safeguarding.action: Record evidence against the adult-at-risk elements and address immediate safety.
safeguarding.record: Identify your reporting responsibility and the authority responsible for enquiries. Use the Wales Safeguarding Procedures and the applicable statutory guidance. Record participation, lawful sharing, accepted responsibilities and review of outcomes. Explain the local-authority and provider complaint processes and relevant advocacy or legal support. A safeguarding referral does not automatically authorise removal, treatment or management of finances. Check the law for the particular proposed action.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions
children.action: Identify the child’s support and protection needs and the relevant Welsh statutory route.
children.record: Hear the child and family with suitable language and communication support. Check who prepares and maintains the IDP and how education, health and social care contributions connect. Plan transition with named responsibilities and confirm actual acceptance by the next service. Disagreement about an ALN decision can involve the applicable reconsideration, disagreement-resolution and Education Tribunal for Wales routes. A social-care complaint follows a different process. Help the family identify the decision and remedy without allowing one dispute to halt other necessary support.

rights.title: Rights, Language and Recording
rights.action: Ask and record language and communication needs and make the Active Offer practical.
rights.record: Identify the actual equality, human-rights and Welsh-language duties of the service. Check the purpose and lawful basis for information sharing, with appropriate limits. Explain access, correction, complaints and the relevant rights or language challenge route. A Welsh-language standards concern, a privacy complaint and a challenge to the care decision may require different bodies. Explain the organisation’s procedure and relevant external route. Address immediate access barriers while a complaint is considered.

foundations.title: Professional Foundations
foundations.action: Check the current Social Care Wales Code and the requirements of the actual role.
foundations.record: Explain the legal or voluntary purpose of involvement and confidentiality limits. Make language, accessibility, power and service barriers visible in assessment. Distinguish a professional concern, service complaint and statutory decision challenge. Social Care Wales addresses professional regulation; the local authority, provider and relevant statutory review bodies address different service decisions. Explain the route that can provide the remedy the person seeks.

sources.record: Record the source, date checked and any uncertainty for supervision.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: Social Care Wales’s new Codes of Professional Practice took effect in July 2026. Use the current worker Code and distinguish it from the employer Code, local-authority procedures and statutory appointments. The professional framework applies across different settings, but the legal power for an intervention depends on the actual function.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: A person’s preferred language and ability to participate belong in the first conversation, formulation and plan. Record how supervision, feedback and professional learning change practice rather than only listing completed training.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Check the current Social Care Wales Code and the requirements of the actual role. Explain the legal or voluntary purpose of involvement and confidentiality limits. Make language, accessibility, power and service barriers visible in assessment. Distinguish a professional concern, service complaint and statutory decision challenge.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Social Care Wales addresses professional regulation; the local authority, provider and relevant statutory review bodies address different service decisions. Explain the route that can provide the remedy the person seeks.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating an old induction handout as the current professional standard.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 separates adult, child and carer assessments in sections 19, 21 and 24. Part 4 and the eligibility regulations govern the next stage; the Part 5 charging decision is separate. Use the current Welsh assessment, meeting-needs, charging and advocacy Codes.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Eligibility requires the applicable needs-and-outcomes analysis and consideration of whether the person can meet those needs alone, with willing others or through accessible community services, or requires the authority’s involvement. A service that exists on a directory but cannot be accessed is not an established solution.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the correct assessment duty and explain the person’s outcomes and evidence of need. Apply the relevant Welsh eligibility regulations rather than a test imported from another system. Check participation barriers and the independent professional advocacy requirements. Record the support plan, separate charging decision, unmet needs and review or complaint route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ask for written reasons and the relevant local-authority review or complaints process. Consider independent advocacy where required to make participation effective. A disagreement over charges should not erase the needs assessment or interim support plan.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using a theoretically available service or an unwilling relative to conclude that a need is already met.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to the specific decision and time. The person must be unable to decide because of an impairment or disturbance of mind or brain; inability concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing relevant information, or communicating the decision. Support must be tried and an unwise choice is not itself incapacity.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An attorney, deputy, advance decision and a professional acting under the Act have different roles and limits. A best-interests decision should preserve participation and consider wishes, feelings, beliefs, values and less restrictive options. It does not itself answer every deprivation-of-liberty or mental-health authority question.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Specify the decision and record support and evidence against the relevant abilities. Explain the causal connection to impairment if concluding that capacity is lacking. Check any attorney, deputy or advance decision and the scope of its authority. Record best-interests reasoning, consultation, disagreement and the appropriate challenge route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Court of Protection deals with relevant disputes and decisions. Consider statutory advocacy requirements and specialist advice where serious disagreement or liberty issues arise. A relative’s agreement should not substitute for the required legal analysis.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating professional disagreement, a diagnosis or a risk score as the capacity test.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Supreme Court’s June 2026 judgment requires the liberty analysis to distinguish the Article 5 consent question from domestic decision-making capacity. The old two-part checklist should not be used as the sole answer. Mere acquiescence does not establish valid consent.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Where required, the hospital or care-home DoLS route and community Court of Protection arrangements have different scope. The actual restrictions, the person’s understanding and wishes, the authorisation and the care or treatment decisions should remain separate in the record.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Record the actual setting, restrictions, duration and response to a wish to leave. Use current judgment and Welsh guidance with specialist advice on the applicable legal test. Check the correct authorisation route, representation, conditions and review. Explore less restrictive alternatives and act on objections or changed circumstances.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the representative, advocacy and court challenge arrangements that apply. An existing authorisation should be reviewed through the responsible process; do not simply remove safeguards on the basis of a changed summary or training slide.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating silence with consent or treating lack of capacity as the complete liberty analysis.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: Use the Mental Health Act 1983 with the Welsh Code of Practice and commenced amendments. The Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010 adds distinct duties concerning primary mental-health support, care coordination and planning, reassessment of eligible former service users and advocacy. It is not simply another detention route.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Part 2 care and treatment planning concerns outcomes, services, responsibilities and review. Part 3 provides a direct reassessment route for eligible former secondary-service users, subject to its conditions. New mental-health reform provisions must be checked for commencement before changing operational procedures.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the exact assessment, detention, treatment or Measure duty involved. Use the Welsh Code and current statutory forms and commencement information. For care planning, record outcomes, named services, responsibilities and review. Explain reassessment and advocacy rights appropriate to the person’s eligibility and status.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Mental Health Review Tribunal for Wales and other statutory review routes address particular detention questions. Measure care planning and reassessment are separate rights. Explain which process addresses the person’s concern and how to obtain support or legal advice.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating every mental-health right as a detention issue or overlooking Measure reassessment duties.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: Section 126 of the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 concerns an adult experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, with care and support needs, who cannot protect themselves because of those needs. The authority’s reasonable-cause-to-suspect enquiry duty and relevant partners’ reporting duties are different.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: A capacity finding is not a substitute for the adult-at-risk analysis. Coercion, dependence, practical barriers and the adult’s own desired outcomes need attention. Reporting, enquiries, service support and authority for any imposed intervention must be distinguished.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Record evidence against the adult-at-risk elements and address immediate safety. Identify your reporting responsibility and the authority responsible for enquiries. Use the Wales Safeguarding Procedures and the applicable statutory guidance. Record participation, lawful sharing, accepted responsibilities and review of outcomes.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the local-authority and provider complaint processes and relevant advocacy or legal support. A safeguarding referral does not automatically authorise removal, treatment or management of finances. Check the law for the particular proposed action.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using capacity as the only safeguarding threshold or treating reporting and enquiries as the same duty.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: Welsh care and support, child protection and education duties need to be mapped separately. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 works alongside the Children Act framework and the Additional Learning Needs and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An Individual Development Plan (IDP) records additional learning needs and provision within the Welsh education framework. It does not replace a care and support plan or child-protection response. Welsh Government published further ALN decision-making guidance and example IDP forms in 2026; use these with the Code and statutory duties.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the child’s support and protection needs and the relevant Welsh statutory route. Hear the child and family with suitable language and communication support. Check who prepares and maintains the IDP and how education, health and social care contributions connect. Plan transition with named responsibilities and confirm actual acceptance by the next service.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Disagreement about an ALN decision can involve the applicable reconsideration, disagreement-resolution and Education Tribunal for Wales routes. A social-care complaint follows a different process. Help the family identify the decision and remedy without allowing one dispute to halt other necessary support.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating an education plan as a substitute for care assessment or a completed transition handover.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Human Rights Act 1998, Equality Act 2010, applicable data-protection law and Welsh-language duties engage different parts of a decision. More than just words promotes the Active Offer of Welsh-language care, recognising language as part of safe and effective support.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Distinguish a person’s language need and the organisation’s applicable Welsh-language standards from a general translation preference. Record how communication affects participation, consent, assessment and the reliability of evidence. A completed English form is not proof that the person could take part effectively.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Ask and record language and communication needs and make the Active Offer practical. Identify the actual equality, human-rights and Welsh-language duties of the service. Check the purpose and lawful basis for information sharing, with appropriate limits. Explain access, correction, complaints and the relevant rights or language challenge route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A Welsh-language standards concern, a privacy complaint and a challenge to the care decision may require different bodies. Explain the organisation’s procedure and relevant external route. Address immediate access barriers while a complaint is considered.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating language access as cosmetic or using a communication barrier as evidence of incapacity.

Approved Mental Health Professional: a statutory role in Mental Health Act processes, exercised through the applicable Welsh arrangements.
The MCA decision-making process for a person lacking capacity for the relevant decision; includes wishes, values, participation and alternatives.
A plan translating assessed needs and outcomes into agreed support, responsibilities and review under the Welsh framework.
The Welsh inspectorate relevant to regulated social care services; safeguarding and other agencies may also need involvement.
The coordinating role within relevant secondary mental health care under the Welsh Measure framework.
Assessment of the carer’s own support needs and outcomes; family care should not simply be assumed.
Pressure or control that may affect the person’s expressed wishes and ability to act freely; requires safe enquiry and careful analysis.
The legal criteria used to determine eligible needs; distinct from the assessment and charging processes.
Individual development plan under the Welsh additional learning needs framework.
Independent Mental Capacity Advocate: a statutory advocacy role for specified circumstances under the MCA framework.
Advocacy supporting participation under the Welsh social services framework; examine barriers and applicable duties.
Consider whether the purpose can be achieved with less interference in rights and freedom.
Welsh legislation addressing primary mental health support, secondary care coordination, assessment for eligible former users and advocacy.
A legal concept relevant to allocating some social care responsibilities; cross-border cases require specific analysis.
A reasoned comparison of the intended benefit, interference with rights and less intrusive alternatives.
The Welsh local authority enquiry duty when there is reasonable cause to suspect an adult at risk in its area.
The relevant-partner duty to report an adult-at-risk concern to the local authority where the statutory conditions apply.
Coordinated preparation for changes in services and adulthood around the young person’s goals and continuity of support.
An approach to understanding the person’s own outcomes, context, strengths and barriers; it does not replace legal assessment duties.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker uses an old professional-code handout and an English-only assessment despite a request for Welsh-language support.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Use the current Code, arrange appropriate communication and revisit any assessment conclusions affected by the barrier. Link the change to supervision and feedback from the person.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Care and Support in Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An authority says community support meets a need, but the only advertised group has no accessible transport or available places.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check actual availability and accessibility in the eligibility reasoning. Revisit whether authority involvement is required, record the unmet need and agree interim action. A directory listing alone does not demonstrate that the outcome can be achieved.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Capacity Act 2005
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult refuses a proposed care arrangement after explaining its benefits and drawbacks, while relatives consider the choice too risky.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Explore the reasoning and support needs without treating disagreement as incapacity. If capacity is lacking, identify the exact authority and best-interests process. Keep the person’s wishes and any liberty issue separately recorded.

scenarioWorkouts.title: DoLS and Deprivation of Liberty
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A resident is quiet during meetings but repeatedly packs a bag and asks staff to take them home.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Use appropriate communication to understand the request and record how staff respond. Review actual restrictions and consent evidence with the responsible specialist. Calm presentation does not settle the legal question or remove the need to support a challenge.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health in Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An eligible former secondary-service user reports deterioration and is told that only a new GP referral can lead to assessment.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the Part 3 conditions and explain the direct reassessment route where applicable. Arrange an appropriate response to urgent need and record responsibility and follow-up. Do not confuse reassessment rights with a guarantee of a particular service.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Safeguarding Adults in Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult understands a relative’s financial demands but relies on that person for meals and fears losing contact if they report.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Consider the protection criteria, dependency and safe ways to hear the adult. Arrange immediate practical help and the appropriate report or enquiries. Understanding the financial transaction does not by itself show that the adult can protect themselves.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A young person has an IDP but no agreed adult support when leaving school, and each service assumes the plan guarantees the other’s provision.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Separate education duties from adult care assessment and service eligibility. Identify the young person’s goals, obtain named decisions and arrange a coordinated transition. The existence of an IDP does not establish that adult social-care support has been agreed.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Language and Recording
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A Welsh-speaking adult appears confused during an English assessment but communicates clearly when suitable Welsh-language support is arranged.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Revisit the evidence and any capacity or eligibility conclusions affected by the communication barrier. Record the support required for future contacts and the person’s account, rather than retaining an unsupported label of confusion.

printableTemplates.title: Care and support assessment
printableTemplates.body:
Care and support assessment
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 separates adult, child and carer assessments in sections 19, 21 and 24. Part 4 and the eligibility regulations govern the next stage; the Part 5 charging decision is separate. Use the current Welsh assessment, meeting-needs, charging and advocacy Codes.

Eligibility requires the applicable needs-and-outcomes analysis and consideration of whether the person can meet those needs alone, with willing others or through accessible community services, or requires the authority’s involvement. A service that exists on a directory but cannot be accessed is not an established solution.

Local pathway:
Identify the correct assessment duty and explain the person’s outcomes and evidence of need.
Apply the relevant Welsh eligibility regulations rather than a test imported from another system.
Check participation barriers and the independent professional advocacy requirements.
Record the support plan, separate charging decision, unmet needs and review or complaint route.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ask for written reasons and the relevant local-authority review or complaints process. Consider independent advocacy where required to make participation effective. A disagreement over charges should not erase the needs assessment or interim support plan.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/contents
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/wsi/2015/1578/contents
https://www.gov.wales/assessing-care-and-support-needs-individuals-code-practice
https://www.gov.wales/advocacy-services-code-practice
https://www.gov.wales/social-services-codes-practice
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.

printableTemplates.title: Decision-specific capacity
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-specific capacity
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies to the specific decision and time. The person must be unable to decide because of an impairment or disturbance of mind or brain; inability concerns understanding, retaining, using or weighing relevant information, or communicating the decision. Support must be tried and an unwise choice is not itself incapacity.

An attorney, deputy, advance decision and a professional acting under the Act have different roles and limits. A best-interests decision should preserve participation and consider wishes, feelings, beliefs, values and less restrictive options. It does not itself answer every deprivation-of-liberty or mental-health authority question.

Local pathway:
Specify the decision and record support and evidence against the relevant abilities.
Explain the causal connection to impairment if concluding that capacity is lacking.
Check any attorney, deputy or advance decision and the scope of its authority.
Record best-interests reasoning, consultation, disagreement and the appropriate challenge route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Court of Protection deals with relevant disputes and decisions. Consider statutory advocacy requirements and specialist advice where serious disagreement or liberty issues arise. A relative’s agreement should not substitute for the required legal analysis.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/contents
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/mental-capacity-act-code-of-practice
https://www.gov.wales/mental-capacity-act-deprivation-liberty-guidance-and-forms
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.

printableTemplates.title: Adult safeguarding: Wales
printableTemplates.body:
Adult safeguarding: Wales
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Section 126 of the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 concerns an adult experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, with care and support needs, who cannot protect themselves because of those needs. The authority’s reasonable-cause-to-suspect enquiry duty and relevant partners’ reporting duties are different.

A capacity finding is not a substitute for the adult-at-risk analysis. Coercion, dependence, practical barriers and the adult’s own desired outcomes need attention. Reporting, enquiries, service support and authority for any imposed intervention must be distinguished.

Local pathway:
Record evidence against the adult-at-risk elements and address immediate safety.
Identify your reporting responsibility and the authority responsible for enquiries.
Use the Wales Safeguarding Procedures and the applicable statutory guidance.
Record participation, lawful sharing, accepted responsibilities and review of outcomes.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the local-authority and provider complaint processes and relevant advocacy or legal support. A safeguarding referral does not automatically authorise removal, treatment or management of finances. Check the law for the particular proposed action.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2014/4/section/126
https://safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a2/a2-p2/
https://www.gov.wales/sites/default/files/publications/2019-06/volume-6-handling-individual-cases-to-protect-adults-at-risk.pdf
https://www.safeguarding.wales/en/adu-i/adu-i-a3pt1/
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.

printableTemplates.title: Liberty and restriction review
printableTemplates.body:
Liberty and restriction review
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Supreme Court’s June 2026 judgment requires the liberty analysis to distinguish the Article 5 consent question from domestic decision-making capacity. The old two-part checklist should not be used as the sole answer. Mere acquiescence does not establish valid consent.

Where required, the hospital or care-home DoLS route and community Court of Protection arrangements have different scope. The actual restrictions, the person’s understanding and wishes, the authorisation and the care or treatment decisions should remain separate in the record.

Local pathway:
Record the actual setting, restrictions, duration and response to a wish to leave.
Use current judgment and Welsh guidance with specialist advice on the applicable legal test.
Check the correct authorisation route, representation, conditions and review.
Explore less restrictive alternatives and act on objections or changed circumstances.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the representative, advocacy and court challenge arrangements that apply. An existing authorisation should be reviewed through the responsible process; do not simply remove safeguards on the basis of a changed summary or training slide.

Sources:
https://supremecourt.uk/cases/press-summary/uksc-2025-0042
https://www.careinspectorate.wales/supreme-court-judgment-deprivation-liberty
https://www.gov.wales/mental-capacity-act-deprivation-liberty-guidance-and-forms
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.

printableTemplates.title: Mental health interface discussion
printableTemplates.body:
Mental health interface discussion
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Use the Mental Health Act 1983 with the Welsh Code of Practice and commenced amendments. The Mental Health (Wales) Measure 2010 adds distinct duties concerning primary mental-health support, care coordination and planning, reassessment of eligible former service users and advocacy. It is not simply another detention route.

Part 2 care and treatment planning concerns outcomes, services, responsibilities and review. Part 3 provides a direct reassessment route for eligible former secondary-service users, subject to its conditions. New mental-health reform provisions must be checked for commencement before changing operational procedures.

Local pathway:
Identify the exact assessment, detention, treatment or Measure duty involved.
Use the Welsh Code and current statutory forms and commencement information.
For care planning, record outcomes, named services, responsibilities and review.
Explain reassessment and advocacy rights appropriate to the person’s eligibility and status.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Mental Health Review Tribunal for Wales and other statutory review routes address particular detention questions. Measure care planning and reassessment are separate rights. Explain which process addresses the person’s concern and how to obtain support or legal advice.

Sources:
https://www.gov.wales/mental-health-act-1983-code-practice
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2010/7/contents
https://www.gov.wales/mental-health-wales-measure-2010-june-2026-html
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/385/contents
https://research.senedd.wales/research-articles/devolution-and-health-in-wales-part-2-mental-health-organ-donation-and-nurse-staffing/
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/mwa/2010/7/part/3
https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/mental-health-bill-2025

printableTemplates.title: Child, family and transition planning
printableTemplates.body:
Child, family and transition planning
Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Welsh care and support, child protection and education duties need to be mapped separately. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 works alongside the Children Act framework and the Additional Learning Needs and Education Tribunal (Wales) Act 2018.

An Individual Development Plan (IDP) records additional learning needs and provision within the Welsh education framework. It does not replace a care and support plan or child-protection response. Welsh Government published further ALN decision-making guidance and example IDP forms in 2026; use these with the Code and statutory duties.

Local pathway:
Identify the child’s support and protection needs and the relevant Welsh statutory route.
Hear the child and family with suitable language and communication support.
Check who prepares and maintains the IDP and how education, health and social care contributions connect.
Plan transition with named responsibilities and confirm actual acceptance by the next service.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Disagreement about an ALN decision can involve the applicable reconsideration, disagreement-resolution and Education Tribunal for Wales routes. A social-care complaint follows a different process. Help the family identify the decision and remedy without allowing one dispute to halt other necessary support.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2018/2/contents
https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-aln-decision-making-and-communication-html
https://www.gov.wales/individual-development-plan-idp-example-standard-form
https://socialcare.wales/resources-guidance/information-and-learning-hub/sswbact/statutory-guidance
https://safeguarding.wales/
https://www.gov.wales/additional-learning-needs-code
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
